pages.title: Pîr-i Turkistan
pages.content: Ahmed Yesevî, known as Pîr-i Turkistan, was the first great Sufi poet to both write and recite his poems in plain Turkish. The word ‘pîr’ in Persian means a Sufi master, spiritual guide, or elder. Yesevî was one of the leading figures of Turkish-Islamic culture and the founder of the Yesevî Order (tarikat, a spiritual path). His poems, called ‘hikmet,’ and the Yesevî Path aimed to spread Islam among the Turks and to teach them the ways of Sufism.

vocabulary.definition: Say a poem or text aloud from memory.
A way of religious and inner life that a group follows.
Make something reach many people or places.

exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that the chapter supports.

replace Persian as the language of literature
unite the Turkic states under one ruler

options: It adds extra information about the poems, like “which are called ‘hikmet’”.
It is the main verb of the sentence.
It shows that someone called the poems.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A past participle clause (called …) can replace a relative clause (which are called …). The commas show that it is extra information.

languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write a paragraph of five to six sentences explaining an honorary title or nickname of a historical figure.

The word ‘mimar’ means architect, but in his case it became part of his name. He was both an engineer and an artist. His works, admired across the world, combine strength with beauty. In my view, the title is deserved because many of his buildings are still standing and in use.”

pages.title: Childhood and Education
pages.content: It is believed that he was born in the town of Sayram in the East Turkestan region in the second half of the 11th century. Having moved to the city of Yesi in Turkestan (now the city of Turkestan in Kazakhstan) at a young age, Ahmed Yesevî studied under Arslan Baba and received a good education. He lived during the era of the Karakhanids (840–1212) and was raised at a time when Turkestan was a center of various fields of knowledge.

exercises.instructions: Read the statement. Is it true or false according to the chapter?

exercises.explanation: Chapter 2: “It is believed that he was born in the town of Sayram …” The writer presents this as a belief, not as a certain fact.

languageFocusExercises.title: Notice: Having Moved …
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Then choose what “Having moved” shows.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Having moved to the city of Yesi in Turkestan at a young age, Ahmed Yesevî studied under Arslan Baba.” What does “Having moved” show?
options: The move happened before he studied under Arslan Baba.
The move happened after he studied.
He moved and studied in different cities at the same time.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Having + past participle” is a perfect participle clause. It shows an action completed before the action in the main clause. Both actions have the same subject.

feedback.incorrect: Which action came first?

languageFocusExercises.title: Build: Was Raised, At a Time When, Now
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct form for each sentence from Chapter 2.

He was raised at a time [choice] Turkestan was a center of knowledge.
[choice] moved to Yesi at a young age, he studied under Arslan Baba.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Raise” (bring up a child) is regular: was raised. Do not confuse it with “rise / rose / risen”. “At a time when” describes a period. “Having + past participle” shows an earlier action.

feedback.incorrect: Check raise / rise, the time word and the participle.

It is believed that he visited the libraries of the city almost every day. The city was a center of art at that time. This setting probably shaped both his taste and his patience.”

pages.title: Teachers and Return to Yesi
pages.content: Some time after Arslan Baba’s death, Ahmed Yesevî traveled to Bukhara, one of the major Islamic centers of the time. There, he came under the guidance and training of Sheikh Yûsuf el-Hemedânî, one of the era’s leading scholars and Sufi masters. This was the master who truly shaped him on the Sufi path (d. 1140). Following the death of his master, Yesevî continued his activities in that region for a time. He then handed over his post as a spiritual guide to Sheikh Abdülhâlik Gucdüvânî, returned to Yesi, and maintained his spiritual guidance until his death.

vocabulary.definition: The most important and respected experts of a subject.
Teachers who guide people on the Sufi path.
Really; in a deep and real way.

pages.content: During this period, he became widely known among the nomadic Turkic communities living in the vicinity of Tashkent (Taşkent) and along the Syr Darya River (Seyhun Nehri). He won the affection of the people through his simple language as well as his words of wisdom (hikmet).

pages.title: The Yesevî Path and the Mausoleum
pages.content:
Among all Turks, particularly the Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Uzbeks, and Turkmen, he is still revered as a spiritual guide under the names Pîr-i Turkistan, Hoca Yesevî, or Ata Yesevî. The Yesevî Order/Path, whose foundations he laid, spread across a vast area extending as far as Anatolia and the Balkans, becoming part of several other orders. Yesevî himself is recognized as the spiritual leader of these orders. At some point between 1389 and 1405, Timur journeyed to the city of Yesi. He visited the tomb of Ahmed Yesevî and subsequently ordered a mausoleum, one of the architectural masterpieces of the era, to be built over the grave. The complex, which included a mosque and a dervish lodge besides the mausoleum, began to take shape, but work came to a stop upon Timur’s death in 1405, leaving the building unfinished. Being buried near the mausoleum of Ahmed Yesevî had a special significance for Central Asian Turks, who led a nomadic lifestyle on the steppes. Because of this, many people purchased plots near the mausoleum during their lifetime with the intention of being buried there. This practice clearly demonstrates the profound influence Ahmed Yesevî had on the Turkic peoples of Central Asia.

In 2003, the historic structure was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List. Its restoration, landscaping, and exterior lighting have been fully completed by TİKA (Turkish Cooperation and Coordination Agency). The complex is currently open to visitors, under protection, and in active use. This mausoleum and complex represent a shared cultural heritage of the Turkic-Islamic world.

The place in the ground where a dead person is buried.
Making the land around a building beautiful.

languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write a paragraph of six to seven sentences about a monument and its history. Use whose and a participle clause.

It has been carefully restored in recent years. Today, it is both a place of worship and a major attraction for visitors.”

pages.title: Language and Identity
pages.content: During Yesevî’s lifetime, Arabic was the language of scholarship and religion, while Persian was the literary language. Although Yesevî knew these languages, he chose Turkish to share his poems, thus contributing to the development of Turkish identity and consciousness within Islamic culture. Ahmed Yesevî was a Hanafi scholar. He received a rigorous madrasa education and thoroughly studied Sufism in addition to the religious sciences. His primary goal was to spread Islam among the Turks and to promote and establish the Ahl al-Sunnah (ehl-i sünnet) creed. As a spiritual guide and moral teacher he also aimed to teach the rulings of Sharia, the principles of Sufism, and the etiquette and practices of his order. Through his disciples, the Sufi path he followed spread far and wide. He sent many of the scholars he trained to the scattered Turkmen tribes, striving to teach them the concepts of statehood and nationhood.

vocabulary.definition: The rules of polite and correct behavior.

languageFocusExercises.question: “Although Yesevî knew these languages, he chose Turkish to share his poems, thus contributing to the development of Turkish identity.” What does “thus contributing” show?

languageFocusExercises.title: Use: Language and Identity Today
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write a paragraph of six to eight sentences arguing how language choice shapes identity today.
languageFocusExercises.question: Should people use global languages or their mother tongue?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: Example: “While English is the main language of science and the internet, our mother tongue remains the language of our hearts. Although many young people prefer English words online, they still dream and pray in their own language. Writers who use their mother tongue keep old words alive, thus protecting a shared memory. Of course, learning global languages opens many doors. However, a community that forgets its language loses part of its identity. Therefore, I believe schools should value both.”

feedback.correct: Check: while, although, thus + -ing and a balanced conclusion.

pages.title: The Path to Fenâʾ fillâh
pages.content: Ahmed Yesevî aimed to convey Islam to Turkish communities during their Islamization process, using simple, straightforward teachings that conveyed profound wisdom and core Islamic values. In particular, he expressed the relationships between Allah, the universe, and humanity in a way that everyone could easily understand. He expressed these ideas in verse, in a new and simple style. The poems were later gathered into the collection known as the Dîvân-ı Hikmet. In this way, he united national elements with religious values and integrated them within the framework of the Qur’an and the Sunnah. According to him, the goal of the path of wisdom is to lead the human being to fenâʾ fillâh. Fenâʾ fillâh is the spiritual state in Sufism in which a believer leaves behind their own ego and worldly desires to live entirely according to the will of Allah. For this, education and the discipline of the self are fundamental. To this end, desires such as greed, selfishness, worldly ambition, and stinginess must be rooted out, while lies, hypocrisy, and backbiting must be rejected. On the other hand, patience, contentment, sincerity, love, and humility must be cultivated. By stressing this aspect of Islam, Ahmed Yesevî emphasized that religion is not merely a matter of sin and reward. Rather, true wisdom manifests itself by transforming a person into a truly human being.

pages.title: Society and Education of Love
pages.content:
In his hikmet (wisdom poems), Ahmed Yesevî conveyed messages not only on religious topics but also on issues of society. Among the topics discussed in his wise sayings are the duty of Muslims to care for orphans and strangers, and the importance of never harming anyone, even non-believers. He also emphasized comforting the heartbroken, standing with the oppressed, and warning against corrupt judges and tyrannical rulers.

Based on this, Yesevî’s approach to education was also centered on love. In his view, teaching a student something properly is only possible by making them love it. People will not accept something they do not love, even if they learn it. For this reason, teachers must treat their students with love and compassion, so that students will truly embrace both the teacher and what they are being taught.

pages.title: The Movement and Its Works
pages.content:
The movement initiated by Ahmed Yesevî in Turkestan quickly flourished and took root in various regions. A broad network of Sufi orders, embraced by thousands of people, spread rapidly and became a major Sufi tradition in Islamic countries, particularly in the Turkic world. Through his disciples, his poems reached even the Turkish tribes living in the remotest corners. In this way, the Yesevî Sufi order spread among the Turks of Central Asia in a short time.

The three major works attributed to Ahmed Yesevî reflect his Sufi thought and teachings: the Dîvân-ı Hikmet, the Fakrnâme, and the Risale der Adab-i Tarikat. However, it should be noted that the current versions of these texts were not written by Yesevî himself. Since these sayings were passed down from one person to another, they were probably written down much later.

Dîvân-ı Hikmet is the title of a collection that contains Yesevî’s poems called ‘hikmet’. It is the foundational text of Turkic Sufi literature. Hikmets are very important because of the significant role they played in the development of the unity of thoughts among Turks.

pages.title: What Is Wisdom?
pages.content:
In the Turkish-Islamic tradition, the term “wisdom” (hikmet) holds a central place. Indeed, the Holy Qur’an is regarded as a source of wisdom itself. The Qur’anic context approaches wisdom from two distinct perspectives. First, as a core goal of education, wisdom, in the sense of knowing the truth, understanding it deeply, and making sound judgments, is one of the most fundamental objectives students are expected to achieve. Second, the Qur’an emphasizes wisdom as a significant gift given by Allah and a defining quality of prophethood. Ultimately, this wisdom fosters vital values such as truthfulness, excellence in work, justice, and living in accordance with one’s sacred knowledge.

Divine religions establish rulings (hüküm) to ensure that people live with faith, morality, and virtue. What is forbidden and what is permitted, as well as the fundamental rulings and principles, were not established merely to serve as rules. According to Makasidü’ş-şeria (the objectives of Islamic law), which aims at protecting life, mind, religion, family, and property, the true reason behind every ruling is wisdom.

Wisdom explains to us the meaning and purpose of every action we take. Without wisdom, obligations and prohibitions become mere formalities. While the rulings established by law seek to answer the questions “What?” and “How?”, wisdom answers the question “Why?” The question “What should I do and how should I do it?” is, of course, important. Whether people are seeking to satisfy their hunger or composing a musical piece, they act in accordance with the answers to the questions “What?” and “How?” However, the question “Why should I do it?” is the fundamental question that gives meaning to all other questions. It is impossible for any action we take to become meaningful without answering the question “Why?” or “For what purpose?”. All obligations and prohibitions find their justification in the wisdom that goes beyond the rules themselves.

In terms of its origin, the word “wisdom” in Arabic means ‘restraint or prevention.’ Wisdom is what protects us from ignorance, from committing shameful acts, and from injustice. The Arabic word for ‘ruling’ (hüküm), which comes from the same root, carries a similar meaning. When it comes to rulings and wisdom, the questions “How?” and “Why?” become intertwined. Without wisdom, even a ruling would become meaningless. As long as the question “Why?” remains unanswered, religious and moral life cannot go beyond formal and mere ritualistic rules.

pages.title: Wisdom in the Qur’an, Justice and Hadith
pages.content:
Many verses in the Qur’an invite believers to look at the universe and at themselves to comprehend the meaning and purpose of all things. If Allah does not create anything without a purpose, He does not want people to do anything without a purpose or meaning either. The fact that everything we do is based on meaning, purpose, and wisdom is one of the fundamental principles of creation. Understanding its purpose and wisdom is an inseparable part of every act of worship.

One verse states: “Allah has revealed to you the Book and wisdom and has taught you what you did not know.” (Surah An-Nisa, 113) It also says, “And indeed, We bestowed wisdom upon Luqman so that he might give thanks to Allah” (Surah Luqman, 12). This means that the Qur’an cannot be understood without wisdom. The verse also states: “Whoever is granted wisdom has been granted a great blessing.” (Surah al-Baqarah, 269). In this sense, there is a connection between Hikmet and “deep understanding,” the technical term for which is ‘fiqh’ (fıkıh). Fiqh does not simply mean ‘law.’ It means ‘to understand thoroughly.’

Wisdom is also closely intertwined with the concept of justice. In other words, those who possess wisdom must be fair. Wisdom is also inseparable from knowledge. Thus, wisdom is a concept closely related to justice, knowledge, and deep understanding.

The hadith that reads, “Wisdom is the lost property of the believer; wherever he finds it, he takes it” (Ibn Mājah, “Zuhd,” 15; Tirmidhī, “ʿIlm,” 19), defines it from another, broader perspective. It also indicates that Muslims should embrace knowledge and truthful words that are useful to them, regardless of who or where they come from.

pages.title: A Civilization of Wisdom
pages.content:
Hoca Ahmed Yesevî illuminated the vast geography stretching from the steppes of Central Asia to Mesopotamia, and from the lands of Anatolia to the Balkans. Great sages who walked the path he paved built a civilization of wisdom in Anatolia. They included Tapduk Emre, Yunus Emre, Mevlana Jalaluddin Rumi, Sadreddin Konevi, Hacı Bektaş-ı Veli, Sarı Saltuk, Baba İlyas, and Somuncu Baba. The sages of Khorasan (Horasan) and the sages of Anatolia, who carried the banner of the Yesevî path, transformed ethnic, geographical, and cultural differences into spiritual richness and a great civilization.

To this day, Ahmed Yesevî’s Dîvân-ı Hikmet remains a spiritual homeland for the Turkic-speaking peoples of Central Asia, despite their division into different political entities and separate physical homelands.

pages.title: From the Dîvân
pages.content:
Here are a few lines from his Dîvân:

“Your scholars do not like your beautiful Turkish

If you listen to the wise, they will enlighten your heart

It would be better for the verses (of the Qur’an) and the sayings of the Prophet to be in Turkish

Those who know their meanings lower their heads.”

“Sevmiyorlar bilginler sizin güzel Türkçe dilini

Bilenlerden işitsen açar gönül ilini

Âyet, hadis anlamı Türkçe olsa duyarlar

Anlamına erenler başı eğip uyarlar”

“Hoca Ahmed is a guide in the garden of spiritual knowledge and wisdom

He tells the truth, opens the land of the heart.

O Poor, Weak Hoca Ahmed! May mercy be upon your seven generations of ancestors,

Although he knows Persian very well, he speaks Turkish so beautifully.”

“Hoca Ahmed, marifet (maneviyat) bostanında kâmil bir mürşiddir (rehberdir);

O hep hakikati söyler ve gönül ülkesinin kapılarını açar.

Ey miskin, zayıf Hoca Ahmed! Senin yedi göbek geçmiş ecdadına rahmet olsun ki;

Farsça dilini çok iyi bildiği halde, Türkçeyi böyle güzelce söylemektedir.”

“Do not harm anybody even if he is an unbeliever, which is the custom of the Prophet,

Even Allah complains about the cold-hearted and the breakers of hearts

For whom Sijjin (Hell) is ready, as Allah is the witness

I narrated these words having heard them from the wise”

“Sünnet imiş, kafir de olsa, incitme sen;

Hüdâ bîzardır (şikayetçidir, uzaktır) katı yürekli gönül incitenden.

Allah şahit, öyle kula hazırdır Siccîn (cehennem);

Bilginlerden duyup bu sözü söyledim işte.”

“How do some people know the value of prayer?

Because, faith renews itself with every prayer,

The heedless man turns his head and sleeps when “As-salat” (prayer!) is announced

Because of heedlessness, he gives his life to the wind, he wastes it.”

“Bazıları namazın kadrini nereden bilir

Her namazda iman baştan tazelenir

‘Es-salat’ dese gafil başını çevirip uyur,

Gafillikten ömrünü yele satar olmalı.”

“Allah’s Messenger asked about the poor, the helpless, and the orphans

On that night, he ascended to the heavens and saw Allah’s beauty

When he returned, he asked about the state of the poor

I descended searching for the traces of the helpless”

“Garip, fakir, yetimleri Resul sordu;

O gece Miraç’a çıkıp Allah cemalini gördü.

Geri gelip indiğinde (yine) fakirlerin halini sordu;

Gariplerin izini arayıp (yer yüzüne) indim ben işte”

exercises.title: Notice: How Certain Is the Writer?
exercises.instructions: Sort the sentences: stated as fact, or presented as believed, attributed or probable?
exercises.question: How certain is the writer?

items: In 2003, the historic structure was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List.
Work came to a stop upon Timur’s death in 1405.
It is believed that he was born in the town of Sayram.
They were probably written down much later.

Stated as fact: In 2003, the historic structure was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List.
Work came to a stop upon Timur’s death in 1405.
Believed, attributed or probable: It is believed that he was born in the town of Sayram.
They were probably written down much later.

exercises.explanation: Recorded dates are stated as facts. “It is believed that” and “probably” signal the writer’s caution.

feedback.incorrect: Look for believed and probably.

exercises.title: Use: Wisdom, Language and Community
exercises.instructions: Write eight to ten sentences on why Yesevî’s ideas still matter, with evidence from two chapters.
exercises.question: Which idea matters most today?
exercises.explanation: Example: “Yesevî’s idea that teaching is only possible through love still matters because students today face great pressure (Chapter 8). It was his simple, straightforward language that won the affection of nomadic communities (Chapter 4). Similarly, teachers who explain complex ideas simply reach more students. Some may argue that modern education needs technology more than warmth. However, technology is only a tool; without care, it cannot inspire anyone. Yesevî also insisted that knowing the reason behind a rule gives it meaning (Chapter 10). This suggests that schools should explain the purpose of what students learn. Therefore, I believe his ideas offer a balanced model: clear language, real purpose and genuine love.”

feedback.correct: Check: evidence from two chapters, a counterpoint and a balanced conclusion.
